paras: The lynching of Epifanio was the hanging of a Mexican prisoner by about thirty masked men near Smithville, Arizona Territory, in late June 1882. The men stopped a deputy sheriff and a district attorney who were taking him from Fort Thomas, seized him and hanged him. The wire report, which attributed the hanging to Mormons, ran in papers from Seattle to Pennsylvania.

The prisoner, named Epifanio in the Phoenix Herald and Epifance in most wire copies, was described as "a noted Mexican horse-thief." According to the Fort Thomas dispatch, he had just come back from Tucson, where he had been treated in the hospital for a gunshot wound in the head. No report describes the theft he was accused of or any court proceeding against him.

Deputy Sheriff G. A. Stevens and District Attorney P. J. Bolan left Fort Thomas with the prisoner on the morning of June 26. About two miles from Smithville they were stopped by about thirty masked men, who took the prisoner and hanged him. The Arizona Weekly Enterprise, which called the men "masked citizens," placed the seizure on Tuesday, June 27.
The dispatch reported that "the citizens generally commend the act," hoping it would serve as "a warning to others." No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story moved as a brief Associated Press item dated Fort Thomas, June 27, and appeared on June 28 in Sacramento, Eureka, Seattle, Salt Lake City and Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Most papers used plain heads such as "Horse Thief Hung" and "Lynching of a Thief," and repeated that the lynchers were "supposed to be Mormons." Some put the Mormons in the headline: the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran "Lynched by Mormons" and the Bismarck Tribune "Hung by Mormons."

The Bismarck Tribune's front-page deck called the victim "A Greaser Horse Thief." Only the longer versions, in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Phoenix Herald, named the officers and passed on the local approval without comment. The Phoenix Herald's text left out the Mormon attribution, while the Arizona Weekly Enterprise kept it in a one-sentence brief on July 1. Later summaries shortened it further, and the Eaton Democrat in Ohio reported only that "Mormons lynched a Mexican horse thief near Smithville, Arizona."

The Bismarck Tribune put the hanging twenty-five miles from Smithville rather than two, and the St. Paul Daily Globe placed Smithville in Utah. The Enterprise called Stevens sheriff rather than deputy sheriff, and the victim's name was printed in at least five spellings.

reader.title: Lynching of Epifanio near Smithville, Arizona
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: About thirty masked men took a prisoner from a deputy sheriff and district attorney on the road and hanged him (A2, A10, A15).

A band of about thirty masked men seized a prisoner described as a 'noted Mexican horse thief' from officers and hanged him, and local citizens were said to 'commend the act' as 'a warning to others' (A2, A10). The victim is described as Mexican, not Black (A2, A15).
The Fort Thomas wire dispatch (A2, A4, A10) and an independent Arizona brief in the Arizona Weekly Enterprise (A15) agree on the seizure from Stevens and the hanging near Smithville.

accounts.label: Wire summary

accounts.label: Arizona Weekly Enterprise
accounts.gist: Masked citizens took a Mexican horse thief from Sheriff Stevens on Tuesday near Smithville and hanged him; supposed Mormons.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the short dispatch under neutral heads such as 'Horse Thief Hung' and 'Lynching of a Thief'.
The full dispatch reported, without dissent, that citizens 'commend the act' and hoped it would be 'a warning to others'.
Eastern and plains papers stressed the supposed Mormon lynchers ('Lynched by Mormons', 'Hung by Mormons'), and the Bismarck Tribune's deck used the slur 'Greaser'.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of one name; the Phoenix Herald gives the Spanish form.
The dispatches dated June 27 are closer to the event; the Enterprise weekly brief may have dated it by the dispatch.
Only the Bismarck Tribune prints twenty-five; likely a telegraphic or typesetting error.
The dispatch is from Fort Thomas, Arizona; 'Utah' in the St. Paul Globe is an error.
The Phoenix Herald's version of the full dispatch omits the Mormon attribution.
